purpose: Structured, source-cited catalogue of documented WML browser behavior divergences from the WAP 1.1/1.2/1.3 spec, gathered for a future historical-compatibility-profile feature. Pure reference data -- no entry here is wired into engine-wasm runtime behavior, and none should be until explicitly promoted per the rules in docs/wml-engine/HISTORICAL_QUIRKS.md.

researchPasses.focus: UP.Browser/Nokia softkey and select-model divergence, WAP Forum GCAG catalogue
researchPasses.note: Wayback Machine was unreachable in this pass; primary vendor documentation (developer.openwave.com, Nokia Forum) was not recoverable, so most entries are unattributed GCAG pattern-tier or tutorial-sourced.

researchPasses.focus: Device-level primary sources: Nokia 7110 service developer guide, Motorola A008 WAP developer style guide, Ericsson R320 manuals, OMA normative specs (WML, WBXML, WMLScript, WMLScript libraries, WAP caching, WAEMT, UAProf), plus contemporary academic/trade-press field testing.
researchPasses.note: URLs and claims transcribed as supplied by the external task, not independently re-fetched/re-verified by the assistant in this integration pass -- if a citation needs re-confirming before being relied on for implementation, treat that as open, not resolved.

entries.claimedBehavior: Some browsers display each anchored element on a separate line; some browsers do not scroll the screen properly when there are many links on the same line.
Some browsers lose the cursor when the screen is scrolled and the anchored text is large.
A list of even a small number of items will flow off the screen of many browsers. While some browsers provide a continuation indication, others do not.
Some browsers' support for select lists is inconsistent past nine items. Some browsers lose cursor context when navigating away from a list and back again.
Some browsers display the title of a link in place of the label for the 'accept' event.
Some browsers display only the first 5 characters of the title of a link/option, and only the first 5 characters of do labels.
Some browsers will load decks from the cache instead of the server if they don't have a different URL (GCAG test example anchor4.cgi).
entries.notes: The one direct, documented caching quirk found in this research pass.

entries.claimedBehavior: Some browsers will display a space for the title even when none is defined; some browsers do not display the title of the card on the screen.
Some browsers display blank options; some display text preceding inputs/selects on a different screen; some do not display anchored text properly on a card whose ordered attribute is false.
Some browsers display all do events on the screen (vs. hiding some under a menu).
entries.notes: Directly relevant to the softkey-model divergence Smethers (2000) describes for Openwave/Phone.com vs Nokia -- see the openwave-select-interaction-model and openwave-6-2-2-do-softkey-assignment entries below.

entries.claimedBehavior: Some browsers display template-defined do events separate from other do events, potentially accessible only by scrolling.
Some browsers only allow one action to be defined for the 'options' event.
Some browsers do not support 'delete' or 'help' events.

Browsers differ in default behaviour when the accept event is not defined. Some browsers do not provide users with a 'back' facility unless the prev action is defined; other browsers have a hard Back key which cannot be programmatically overridden.
entries.notes: The clearest documented hardware-vs-programmatic navigation divergence found: a hard Back key bypassing WML navigation semantics entirely on some devices.

entries.claimedBehavior: On some browsers, do events of generic, experimental, or vendor-specific types are displayed as blank links.
entries.notes: Direct evidence that vendor-specific do-type extensions were a real, if fragile, practice -- see also up-browser-vendor-specific-tags below.

entries.claimedBehavior: Some browsers display labels near the keys corresponding to these events; if spaces are present in the label it can look like an unlabeled key is labelled.
Few browsers implement fieldsets. Where they are supported, fieldsets interfere with browser display of other elements.
The smallest screen width of the browser that supports images is 81 pixels; the smallest screen height that supports images is 44 pixels.
entries.notes: Concrete numeric constraint derived from real device testing (GCAG Table 2/3 device list), not a vague generality.

entries.claimedBehavior: Locally defined images (client-resident icon substitution) are different for different browsers.
entries.notes: Confirms localsrc was real but non-portable across vendors.

entries.claimedBehavior: All browsers that support images support the wireless bitmap (WBMP) type, but not necessarily any other image type.

In some browsers, selecting the default option does not trigger onpick. Some browsers don't handle option items mixed with onpick well. Multi-select + onpick combination is implemented differently across browsers and behaves inconsistently.
onenterbackward, when used for navigation, adversely interferes with the history stack, unexpectedly trapping the user in the new card.
entries.notes: The clearest documented navigation-history divergence found. Directly relevant to WaveNav's history/back-stack semantics.

entries.wmlConstruct: text entities (soft hyphen, non-breaking space), anchored text styling
entries.claimedBehavior: Soft hyphens are not usefully supported by most browsers. Non-breaking spaces do not work on every browser -- some treat them as breaking spaces. Underscores in anchored text are obscured because some browsers underline anchored text.
Anchored text may destroy the format of a table. Nowrap-mode overflow cannot be viewed in some browsers. GCAG's general recommendation is to avoid tables entirely.

The first do[type=accept] in a card becomes the left softkey; a second accept-type do becomes the right softkey; additional accept-type do elements are pushed into a menu. The first do[type=options] becomes the right softkey; if multiple options-type do elements exist it is labeled 'Menu'. Contrasted against Nokia Mobile Browser 4.0 and Sony Ericsson T610/T68i, which surface dedicated Options/Menu softkeys regardless of do ordering.
entries.notes: Named version (6.2.2) with a specific, falsifiable rule, but a secondary/tutorial source, not an Openwave primary document or independently reproduced test. Do not implement as runtime behavior without independent corroboration.

entries.claimedBehavior: Some devices interpret WML's select element as a popup menu list; others interpret it as a menu usable for navigation. Contrasted explicitly against Nokia by a Phone.com employee: an application written for Nokia won't run in a usable manner on a Phone.com browser or other 3rd-party browsers.
entries.notes: Paul Smethers, Phone.com Inc., W3C Digital Imaging/Appliances workshop paper, October 2000. High confidence the divergence existed (insider source, names Nokia explicitly); medium confidence on exact mechanics -- does not specify precisely which UI Phone.com's own browser used vs Nokia's, only that they differed.

entries.claimedBehavior: UP.Browser supported carrier- and vendor-specific tags beyond the WML spec (e.g. custom KDDI and J-Phone tags). Microsoft's ASP.NET mobile-controls framework shipped a distinct UpWmlPageAdapter / UpWmlMobileTextWriter specifically to work around UP.Browser-specific rendering behavior.
entries.notes: Confirms vendor-specific extensions existed as a category, not which tags/attributes specifically. The OSnews source (2006) postdates this project's WML-1.1/1.2 target era (1999-2001) by 5+ years -- chronology mismatch, flagged explicitly. Secondary corroboration: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/aspnet/t32t3y06(v=vs.100) confirms the UpWmlPageAdapter existed but not its specific compensations.

entries.claimedBehavior: Openwave's WML implementation reportedly carried forward extensions from its predecessor HDML (Handheld Device Markup Language) to ease migration of existing HDML sites.
entries.sourceUrl: https://thewirelessfaq.com/ (page '7.17 What are Openwave WML Extensions and how do they work?' -- returned HTTP 403, not read)
entries.notes: Plausible and repeated across several tutorial-tier sources, but no primary or detailed secondary account of which specific extensions resulted could be read in this research pass. Concrete follow-up target: retry fetching thewirelessfaq.com with a different method, or find a mirror.

entries.wmlConstruct: img content-type support (simulator vs. reference reader)
entries.claimedBehavior: The UP simulator reportedly handled only the BMP image format, while the DSR Wireless Application Reader accepted only GIF images, when the same WML application was evaluated across three WAP platforms.
entries.sourceUrl: Kaasinen, Aaltonen, Kolari, Melakoski, Laakko, "Two Approaches to Bringing Internet Services to WAP Devices," WWW9, May 2000 (VTT Information Technology) -- paper itself could not be fetched (archive.thewebconf.org unreachable, ScienceDirect 403)
entries.notes: This claim comes from a search-engine-generated summary, not text read directly. Explicitly unverified -- treat as 'worth chasing down,' not established fact, until someone reads the actual paper (VTT research portal / ResearchGate / Academia.edu mirrors were surfaced but not fetched).

entries.claimedBehavior: Options are accessed via a left 'Options' softkey; template-based menus surface through the device's dedicated Options softkey regardless of do declaration order (contrast with Openwave's ordering-sensitive left/right/menu assignment).
entries.notes: Same source and confidence caveats as openwave-6-2-2-do-softkey-assignment. Nokia Mobile Browser 4.0 is a mid-2000s device, later than the WML-1.1/1.2 era this project's compliance program most directly targets -- chronology caveat applies.

entries.wmlConstruct: XML/WML error tolerance, simulator vs. real device
entries.claimedBehavior: Nokia's WAP Toolkit is commonly claimed to be more tolerant of XML errors than real devices, such that some pages that pass in the simulator would not display properly on an actual phone.
entries.notes: Unsourced claim on the citing page. Nokia's own WAP Toolkit 1.2 Developer's Guide (https://www.readkong.com/page/developer-s-guide-9421654) was fetched directly and does NOT itself disclose any simulator-vs-hardware divergence -- this entry is included as a commonly-repeated claim, not a corroborated one. The general phenomenon (SDK simulators being more permissive than real embedded hardware) is plausible and common for the era but should not be treated as Nokia-specific until corroborated.

entries.product: Nokia WAP Toolkit 1.2, Ericsson WapIDE 2.0, Phone.com UP.SDK
entries.claimedBehavior: Contemporary comparison describes Nokia's WAP Toolkit 1.2 as a Windows NT4-only, Java2-runtime-dependent single integrated IDE with a superior UI to Ericsson's WapIDE 2.0, which required separate applications plus bundled Perl 5.0/Tcl-Tk/the Xitami web server.
entries.notes: Tooling/workflow evidence, not in-browser rendering divergence -- included as context for why content targeting one vendor's SDK often diverged from another's in practice. Page shows a September 2023 CMS timestamp (almost certainly a re-platforming date, not original publication date); internal content reads as contemporaneous with WAP Toolkit 1.2 / UP.SDK 4.0 (circa 1999-2000), but original publication date could not be independently confirmed (Wayback Machine blocked in the research session).

entries.wmlConstruct: table and other tags, general interpretation strictness
entries.claimedBehavior: wApua (a hobbyist WML browser/debugger) was built partly out of frustration with commercial WML browsers including WinWAP, and its README states wApua interprets some tags that WinWAP 2.2/2.3 interpret 'very rudimentary or even wrong, e.g. tables.'
entries.notes: WinWAP is a PC-based desktop WML browser, not UP.Browser or Nokia's mobile browser -- different vendor category from the rest of this file, but direct, named, versioned developer testimony about real WML interoperability pain in the era, so included for completeness.

entries.claimedBehavior: 96x65 pixel display, four main content lines, max 96x44 graphics area, proportional 8-pixel fonts, a roller for focus/activation, left softkey labeled Options, right softkey labeled Back. Links were always placed on separate lines. Scrolling did not wrap from the final item back to the first.
entries.notes: Nokia service developer guide, pass 2 research. Foundational device profile -- most early European WAP content was authored/tested against this device.

entries.claimedBehavior: do elements appeared, in source order, merged into the phone's native options menu between the context-sensitive Select/Edit command and the native Use Number, Empty Cache, and Exit commands. Authored actions did not necessarily become visible softkeys -- they could be buried inside the phone's existing menu structure.
A prev task was mapped to the right softkey as the localized Back command, but the 7110 did not display that softkey when the history stack was empty, even when the deck defined the action.
entries.notes: Directly relevant to WaveNav's back-button/navigation-history UI state -- a real device would conditionally hide, not just disable, the back affordance.

entries.claimedBehavior: Activating a select opened a dedicated modal list screen, not an inline widget. Multiple selections used Mark/Unmark, with Done on the right softkey.
entries.notes: Suggested as a real UI state transition (CARD_VIEW -> SELECT_EDITOR -> CARD_VIEW), not a text box overlay.

entries.claimedBehavior: Inputs opened dedicated number, text, or password editor screens based on the format and type attributes. In the number editor, pressing '*' twice entered a plus sign. Long input titles were truncated to one line.

entries.wmlConstruct: native browser extension, not a WML construct
entries.claimedBehavior: The browser scanned the currently displayed card for number-like strings. Selecting 'Use Number' from the menu let the user pick a discovered number and exit to the phone's standby/dialer interface with that number ready to call, save, or use in an SMS -- without the author marking it with a tel: URI.
entries.notes: Nokia-only native extension with no WML markup trigger -- a strong, self-contained candidate for a simulated phone-shell transition if this profile is ever built.

entries.wmlConstruct: b, i, u, big, small, em, strong
entries.claimedBehavior: Styling elements (b, i, u, big, small, em, strong) were ignored entirely. Tabs became spaces.
A linked bitmap was not rendered as a clickable image -- its alt text became the visible link text instead. A missing image produced a small default placeholder picture.
entries.notes: Example: should render as a plain text link reading 'Buy', not a clickable image, under this profile.

entries.claimedBehavior: Tables were effectively linearized into a sequence of cells (no real grid rendering). Fieldset grouping could fail silently when the grouped content did not fit the display.
Images that fit the display were centered. Oversized images were aligned top-left and clipped rather than scaled. Text could not appear beside an image.

entries.wmlConstruct: device firmware revision -- affects img, table, direct URL entry, OTA bookmarks
entries.claimedBehavior: Firmware 4.94 materially changed browser behavior: added/improved horizontal alignment, table rendering, images used as links, scrolling of tall images, direct URL entry, browser settings for wrapping/image display, and OTA bookmarks over SMS.
entries.notes: Recommends splitting into two distinct profiles (nokia_7110_pre_4_94 / nokia_7110_4_94_plus) rather than treating firmware as decorative metadata -- a real example of a device changing its effective WML dialect after release via a firmware update, not a new device.

entries.claimedBehavior: Total cache 32.5 KB; maximum individual cache entry 1,536 bytes; URLs longer than 128 bytes were not cached; maximum compiled deck or image item approximately 1.3 KB; maximum 15 bookmarks.
entries.notes: Contemporary (B-tier) field material separately quotes a 1,397-byte compiled-deck limit and reports an oversized deck could freeze the browser until restart -- that failure mode should map to a deterministic HistoricalFailure-style diagnostic outcome if ever implemented, never an actual hang. See the 'what not to reproduce literally' guidance in COMPATIBILITY_PROFILE_DESIGN_NOTES.md.

entries.claimedBehavior: The Nokia 7110 automatically inserted line breaks after links and input fields; the Ericsson R320 required an explicit br to create an equivalent layout. Developers either generated device-specific WML or accepted that identical decks would have visibly different spacing across the two devices.
entries.notes: Named, contrasted, falsifiable claim from contemporary field testing (academic). A strong compatibility-fixture candidate.

entries.claimedBehavior: 101x65 pixel display with pixels approximately 24% taller than they are wide (non-square pixels). Full browser view showed four content rows plus a header; input/selection views used three content rows plus a header. Tall images could be vertically scrolled; images wider than the display were horizontally truncated.
entries.notes: A faithful renderer for this profile should not assume square pixels -- a nominally square WBMP would appear physically taller on the real device.

entries.claimedBehavior: Ericsson recommended UTF-8 but warned that handset software varied by market -- a phone could support displaying a character while not supporting entering that same character in a WAP form.
entries.notes: Suggests separating display_charset / input_charset / wmlscript_native_charset as distinct concepts rather than one crate-wide notion of 'the charset'.

entries.claimedBehavior: Contemporary field references put the R320's compiled-deck capacity around 3,000 bytes, considerably larger than the Nokia 7110's common-denominator ~1.3-1.4 KB limit.
entries.notes: Useful for distinguishing content authored for the broad market vs. Ericsson-class devices specifically.

entries.product: Ericsson WAP phones (general, era of R320)
entries.claimedBehavior: Ericsson WAP phones reportedly rejected URLs containing literal spaces, including some WMLScript examples distributed with Nokia's own developer toolkit.
entries.notes: 'Ericsson WAP phones' generally, not R320-specific -- attribution confidence medium rather than high for that reason.

entries.claimedBehavior: UP.Browser tried to map the primary do[type=accept] action directly to a softkey, unlike Nokia's menu-burial approach. A single options action could occupy another softkey; multiple options actions caused the browser to generate a menu or pseudo-card. When a link gained focus, its title/action could take control of the Accept key.
entries.notes: Proposed arbitration order: (1) focused link/field action, (2) card-level accept, (3) card-level options, (4) generated options menu, (5) browser-native commands. This is a real algorithm, not fixed button labels -- available physical keys vary by handset (see the Motorola A008 and OEM-overlay entries).

entries.product: UP.Browser (same version, different OEM handsets: Siemens S35, Motorola V.2288)
entries.claimedBehavior: A contemporary field study found a Siemens S35 and a Motorola V.2288, running the identical UP.Browser version, disagreed on the big element: Siemens rendered it (effectively as bold), Motorola ignored it entirely.
entries.notes: Structurally important finding: a UA string like 'UP.Browser/4.1' alone is not sufficient to select a rendering profile -- an OEM handset overlay is needed on top of the engine profile (e.g. openwave_up_4_1 + siemens_s35_overlay vs. + motorola_v2288_overlay).

entries.wmlConstruct: HTTP/WSP request headers, not WML markup
entries.claimedBehavior: A real logged UP.Browser 4.1 request advertised detailed device-capability headers: x-up-devcap-max-pdu, x-up-devcap-iscolor, x-up-devcap-numsoftkeys, x-up-devcap-screenpixels, x-up-devcap-screendepth, x-up-devcap-charset, x-up-devcap-msize, x-up-devcap-smartdialing, x-up-devcap-immed-alert, x-up-subno, plus supported content types (WML, compiled WML, WMLScript, WBMP, HDML, BMP, Phone.com alert/cache-operation types, other Unwired Planet formats).
entries.notes: Origin services historically used these headers to tailor decks -- worth generating from the selected device profile and surfacing in a protocol inspector if a compatibility-profile feature is ever built, not just historical trivia.

entries.claimedBehavior: UP.Browser retained strong HDML/Unwired Planet ancestry, including Phone.com-specific MIME types: application/x-up-alert, application/x-up-cacheop, application/x-up-device, application/x-up-digestentry, application/x-hdmlc.
entries.notes: Some services depended on this ecosystem beyond standard WML. Good candidate for an experimental extension module rather than the core WML parser if ever implemented.

entries.claimedBehavior: Phone.com/Openwave extensions reportedly included exit and link elements requiring a Phone.com-specific DTD (-//PHONE.COM//DTD WML 1.1//EN vs. the standard -//WAPFORUM//DTD WML 1.1//EN), and the ability to place images inside option elements when using that DTD.
entries.sourceUrl: not individually re-verified in this pass -- supplied by external research task without a single pinned URL for this specific claim
entries.notes: Explicitly flagged by the source research as contemporary but less authoritative than the surviving device guides -- marked experimental/B-confidence there too. Unknown Phone.com extensions should not silently become standard WML behavior; register vendor DTDs/tokens separately if implemented.

entries.claimedBehavior: Exposed four browser controls (Left: Options, Center-left: Back, Center-right: Browser menu, Right: Accept), labels limited to six characters. Touchscreen device, 240x320 display, 240x236 WAP content area, eight rows of Western text. Reported UA: MOT-F6/10.36.32 UP.Browser/4.1.23d.
entries.notes: An entirely different interaction surface from a two-softkey Nokia device -- direct evidence a fixed 'softkey count' assumption in a compatibility model would be wrong.

entries.wmlConstruct: input, p (content flow after an input field)
entries.claimedBehavior: Elements following an input field were not displayed until that input field had been accepted/committed. The device otherwise allowed text, links, input fields, and images on the same line.
entries.notes:
The most unusual A008-specific behavior found across both research passes. Example:

Name: Welcome, $(name) Continue

-- under this profile the initial card should stop visually at the input; 'Welcome, $(name)' and the Continue link should appear only after the editor commits.

entries.claimedBehavior: Horizontal marquee-like text scrolling ('Times Square'). No horizontal or vertical image scrolling. Paragraph alignment supported. Tables rendered without borders, with left/top cell padding and left-only cell alignment. Monospace 15x16 font. Soft hyphen always visibly rendered. WBMP images only, no images used as links.

entries.wmlConstruct: deck size, cache, cookies, push, WTAI
entries.claimedBehavior: Approximately 5,000-byte maximum deck size, but only about the first 3,800 text characters were displayed. Persistent 64 KB cache with a default 30-day expiry. Cookies supported only when routed through an UP.Link gateway. No push or menu-timer support. WTAI call support with WAP suspend/resume.

Motorola's own test matrix records many Windows-1252-range characters rendering as blank, codepoints beyond 255 producing '?', and the soft hyphen always rendering visibly. A literal dollar sign had to be represented as two dollar signs ($$) because of WML variable-substitution syntax.
entries.notes: Motorola's own documented test matrix -- unusually direct primary evidence for character-level rendering bugs. Suggests per-profile character rendering should be a mapping table, not just 'decode UTF-8 and draw Unicode.'

entries.claimedBehavior: UP.Browser 4.1 included 175 local built-in icons addressable through the standard localsrc attribute (arrows, warning marks, clocks, weather symbols, mail, phones, trains, boats, dice, batteries, meals, tools, various UI glyphs). alt remained required. The browser could use the built-in icon without fetching the referenced image at all.
entries.notes: Example: . Cataloging the full 175-icon set would be a highly visible, relatively self-contained authenticity feature if this profile is ever built -- the icon list itself was not transcribed into this entry and would need to be sourced from the style guide directly.

entries.claimedBehavior: Supported bold and italic. big was effectively displayed as bold. An oversized deck was truncated to the portion that fit, rather than producing the Nokia-7110-style reported freeze.
entries.sourceUrl: not individually re-pinned by the external research task beyond general field-test attribution
entries.notes: Evidence tier B per the source research (contemporary field testing, not a primary vendor document recovered directly). Useful as one of (at least) three distinct oversized-deck behaviors documented across profiles: reject-with-error (implied elsewhere), truncate-at-compiled-boundary (this device), and Nokia's possible-freeze.

entries.wmlConstruct: network/gateway latency, not a WML construct
entries.claimedBehavior: A real service test over a 9,600 bit/s GSM CSD connection (T-Mobile/T-D1) recorded approximately: 16s before the welcome page appeared, 24s before the first input step, 38s at the detailed form, 43s for the result, 51s for contact details, 57s to reach the final vCard operation.
entries.sourceUrl: not individually re-pinned by the external research task beyond general field-test attribution
entries.notes: Not device-specific behavior -- a period network/gateway latency data point. Suggested as an optional CSD-timing simulation mode (network.profile = gsm_csd_9600), not the default development experience. Should not be conflated with a device rendering quirk; kept here for cross-reference since it came from the same field test.

entries.claimedBehavior: A hotlink (anchor) automatically received a line break. An explicit br placed directly after an anchor was ignored/absorbed -- authors needed two br elements to actually create a visible empty line between links.
entries.sourceUrl: supplied by external research task; specific Nokia Series 40 developer guide not individually re-pinned in this pass
entries.notes:
Ideal compatibility fixture pair: One
Two -> no blank line under this profile; One

Two -> exactly one blank line.

entries.claimedBehavior: Unlike the early 7110's linearized tables, Series 40 rendered real bordered rows and columns. Cell widths were dynamic with a minimum width applied; oversized cell content could be truncated with an ellipsis; full cell content could be inspected by scrolling or explicitly selecting the row.
entries.sourceUrl: supplied by external research task; specific Nokia Series 40 developer guide not individually re-pinned in this pass
entries.notes: Implies a selectable/scrollable table interaction state, not just a different layout algorithm from the 7110 profile.

entries.claimedBehavior: 128x128 display, 122x96 application area, five main text lines. Supported WBMP, static GIF, and animated GIF (up to 13 frames, ~2.4 KB max size), four-direction image viewing, a picture viewer for oversized images, and a browser setting to disable images entirely. Image links displayed with a full-line frame. When a link was focused, the browser added 'Open link' to its options menu; do elements lived in the options list; prev could populate both the right Back softkey and the options list.
entries.sourceUrl: supplied by external research task; specific Nokia Series 40 developer guide not individually re-pinned in this pass
entries.notes: Treat as a later evolutionary profile distinct from the 7110, not a color-screen skin of it -- richer table/image/menu model throughout.

entries.wmlConstruct: deck size, cache size (documentation ambiguity, not a rendering behavior)
entries.claimedBehavior: The scanned Nokia developer guide literally prints resource figures as '2.8kbit' for deck size and '20kbit' for cache size -- ambiguous whether this means kilobits, a typo for kilobytes, or something else.
entries.sourceUrl: supplied by external research task; specific Nokia Series 40 developer guide not individually re-pinned in this pass
entries.notes: Explicitly flagged by the source research as an unresolved archival ambiguity -- retain the literal source datum and flag the byte conversion as unresolved rather than quietly hard-coding a guessed 2.8 KB figure if this is ever implemented.

entries.claimedBehavior: WML defined a single browser context containing variables, navigation history, and implementation-specific state. newcontext="true" removed all variables, cleared history, and reset implementation-specific state. Variables were not domain-specific in the modern browser-storage sense -- they could persist after leaving a service, and an unrelated application could accidentally reuse the same variable names and encounter values left behind by a different service.
entries.notes: Historically important but privacy-hostile by modern standards. Proposed as three explicit modes: StrictHistoricalBrowserContext (global, cross-service, matches the spec), IsolatedPerOrigin, IsolatedPerDeck -- with StrictHistoricalBrowserContext available only in an explicitly labeled laboratory/legacy profile, never a default. This is a normative WML 1.1 spec requirement, not a vendor quirk -- distinct in kind from most other entries in this file.

entries.claimedBehavior: WML history entries stored the absolute card URL, GET/POST method, POST fields, and request headers -- not the rendered card content itself. Variable references were resolved before being stored. Every explicit card navigation pushed an entry, even when identical to the previous one. Returning to a deck originally fetched via POST could require the user agent to reissue the original POST data.
entries.notes: Suggests a HistoryEntry{card_url, method, post_fields, request_headers} shape rather than a RenderedCardSnapshot -- materially different from a modern visual back-stack model. Normative WML 1.1 spec requirement.

entries.claimedBehavior: The onenterbackward event fired when a card was entered via history/prev navigation. A card-level onenterbackward event handler overrode the deck-level (template) handler, even when the two used different syntaxes.
entries.notes: Normative WML 1.1 spec requirement, not a vendor quirk -- worth double-checking against current engine-wasm onenterbackward/template precedence handling as a possible spec-fidelity gap independent of any compatibility-profile feature.

entries.claimedBehavior: The spec recommended constrained devices delete least-recently-used history entries under memory pressure, suggesting a minimum history depth of ten. If variable/context memory was exhausted, the user agent could reclaim cache and history, notify the user, clear context, or return to a known state.
entries.notes: Normative but non-mandatory ("could") spec guidance. Suggested as a deterministic resource-pressure test sequence: evict cache -> evict oldest history -> retry -> emit historical out-of-memory event -> reset to a configured known state.

entries.claimedBehavior: The spec explicitly allowed a small-screen browser to present an unordered card's fields as separate screens -- transformed into a hierarchical summary screen where individual fields were selected for editing, rather than rendered inline top-to-bottom.
entries.notes: ordered="false" should not be treated as a decorative hint. Suggests a FormPresentation enum (Inline, SequentialEditors, SummaryThenEditor) selected by the active compatibility profile. Normative WML 1.1 spec requirement.

entries.claimedBehavior: A requested accesskey was only a hint. The user agent was not required to support access keys at all, could choose a different available key than the one requested, and could ignore further access-key requests once available keypad assignments were exhausted.
entries.notes: An authentic access-key rendering must come from a final key-allocation pass at render time, not read directly off the WML attribute. Normative WML 1.1 spec requirement.

entries.claimedBehavior: WML timers were specified in tenths of a second, but actual timer resolution and interaction with the UI was implementation-dependent. A timer could restart around certain refresh transitions. Authors were explicitly instructed not to depend on exact timing.
entries.notes: Suggests a per-profile timer quantization concept (timer_tick_ms, timer_dispatch_granularity_ms, pause_timer_while_editor_open) rather than assuming the same fine-grained timer behavior everywhere -- a strict-conformance profile and a handset-emulation profile may legitimately differ here. Normative WML 1.1 spec requirement, relevant to WaveNav's existing deterministic-timer design goal even outside a compatibility-profile feature.

entries.wmlConstruct: gateway pipeline: XML parse, DTD/structural validation, WBXML compile
entries.claimedBehavior: WML was XML and was commonly compiled into WBXML at the gateway. Invalid element ordering or DTD violations could cause gateway-side compilation to fail entirely, leaving no page for the handset to display at all -- not a rendered error page, just nothing.
entries.notes: Suggests a layered gateway failure taxonomy distinguishing origin_http_error / origin_wrong_mime / gateway_xml_parse_failure / gateway_wml_validation_failure / gateway_wbxml_compile_failure / terminal_wbxml_decode_failure -- a generic 'page failed to load' collapses historically meaningful distinctions.

entries.claimedBehavior: Common historical content types: text/vnd.wap.wml, application/vnd.wap.wmlc, text/vnd.wap.wmlscript, application/vnd.wap.wmlscriptc, image/vnd.wap.wbmp. Nokia explicitly documented these mappings; period server guidance separately described Phone.com-specific alert/cache-operation types (see openwave-hdml-proprietary-mime-types).
entries.notes: A compatibility gateway profile should not automatically forgive text/html or text/plain content unless the selected gateway profile historically performed that conversion -- MIME strictness was operationally significant, not incidental.

entries.claimedBehavior: Even a precompiled .wmlc deck still passed through the WAP gateway, because the gateway translated between HTTP and WAP requests/responses regardless of whether WML-to-WBXML compilation itself was needed. Gateways could also cache compiled decks.
entries.notes: Relevant to Lowband's real WSP stack: 'precompiled' should bypass WML-to-WBXML compilation specifically, not bypass the gateway/session layer entirely.

entries.wmlConstruct: WSP session/capability negotiation, not a WML construct
entries.claimedBehavior: WSP was effectively a binary, session-oriented HTTP-family protocol supporting compact headers, typed content, persistent session headers, capability negotiation, push, multipart-equivalent objects, and simultaneous asynchronous transactions.
entries.sourceUrl: supplied by external research task, general WSP characterization not individually re-pinned to a single spec section in this pass
entries.notes: A gateway/transport model should not treat WSP as a stateless HTTP transcoder -- it can retain negotiated capabilities across requests and across suspend/resume cycles. Relevant to Lowband's connection-oriented WSP design (see the WTP research memo, Part 2) beyond just the compatibility-profile feature.

entries.claimedBehavior: UAProf information and profile differences could be cached for the lifetime of a WSP session; a device could update its profile on resume. A gateway could add network-derived information or override device-provided values according to operator policy. HTTP-profiled devices used x-wap-profile and x-wap-profile-diff headers.
entries.notes: Suggests a layered profile-resolution stack: device capabilities + firmware capabilities + SIM/network capabilities + operator gateway overrides + request-specific Profile-Diff -- a period-correct content-negotiation mechanism, distinct from (and complementary to) the browser-rendering CompatibilityProfile concept.

entries.claimedBehavior: WAP's caching model was based on HTTP/1.1 but explicitly accounted for low-end devices including zero-byte-cache devices. Gateways were expected to act as faithful caching proxies and maintain reliable time; X-WAP-TOD was available to synchronize clients that lacked a trustworthy clock.
entries.notes: A high-fidelity cache implementation would need to model terminal clock, gateway clock, origin Date/Age/Expires, terminal clock skew, and X-WAP-TOD synchronization separately -- more historically accurate than using the host computer's current wall clock everywhere.

entries.claimedBehavior: The WBMP specification recommended examining the actual WBMP header and allowing its TypeField to take precedence over a conflicting MIME 'level' parameter.
entries.notes: Deliberate historical sniffing rule: if Content-Type says WBMP level 1 but the WBMP header's TypeField says type 0, decode as type 0 (with a diagnostic), not per the MIME parameter.

entries.claimedBehavior: WBXML carries its own charset field, but external WSP/HTTP/MIME character information may also be present and can conflict. A charset field value of zero means no encoding information is supplied at all. Binary transformation to WBXML also discards document-level metadata such as the original DTD representation.
entries.notes: Suggests decoded decks should retain charset provenance (WspContentType / HttpContentType / WbxmlHeader / XmlDeclaration / ProfileDefault) to make character-encoding bugs diagnosable, rather than collapsing to a single resolved charset with no history of where it came from. Directly relevant to transport-rust's wbxml_decoder.rs charset precedence handling (already partly covered in Pass 4 of the 2026-07-25 architecture review) -- worth cross-checking as a possible fidelity gap independent of the compatibility-profile feature.

entries.claimedBehavior: Textual WMLScript was compiled into WMLScript bytecode before being interpreted -- the handset interpreter consumed bytecode compilation units, not source text evaluated directly the way JavaScript typically is.
entries.notes: engine-wasm/engine's existing wavescript module already models this correctly (decode_compilation_unit consumes bytecode, per the architecture review's Pass 2/5 findings) -- this entry documents the normative justification for that design, it does not identify a gap. Suggested pipeline stages if a protocol/debug inspector is ever built: .wmls source -> WMLScript compiler -> .wmlsc bytecode -> bytecode verifier -> interpreter, with the transition visible even when the compiler is embedded locally for convenience.

entries.claimedBehavior: Nominal 'WAP 1.1 support' did not guarantee identical WMLScript behavior. Period desktop simulators frequently omitted WMLScript or WTAI entirely, while vendor SDKs varied in completeness; Nokia's beta toolkit was itself reported to freeze and mishandle some WMLScript output. The standard library itself contained optional behavior -- e.g. immediate WMLBrowser.refresh support was explicitly optional in the spec.
entries.notes: Argues against a single wmlscript_supported: bool flag in favor of a capability set (bytecode_version, compiler_available, interpreter_available, standard_libraries, immediate_refresh, wtai_functions, max_stack_depth, max_compilation_unit_bytes) if a compatibility-profile feature is ever built. The WMLBrowser.refresh-is-optional claim in particular is a normative spec fact worth checking against engine-wasm's current wavescript stdlib implementation independent of the profile feature.
